column2: This file covers whole-item packing: when a batch exceeds a channel limit, truncate **by whole items**
and accurately report excluded counts so callers mark only actually delivered entries.
Previously the full rendered body was truncated and the entire batch marked delivered: later entries disappeared,
while history showed total success, silently losing vulnerabilities with no way to detect it.
A 200-item Chinese batch necessarily exceeds WeCom's 4096-byte limit.
The header must accurately report included and remaining counts, or readers assume the header
number covers everything.
Include only the first kept items.
0 = unlimited.
Even if the budget cannot fit one item, send one anyway and rely on final truncation.
Otherwise one oversized vulnerability permanently blocks the batch: every claim fits nothing and sends nothing.
An empty message has no deliverable entries.
Telegram limits **characters**; counting bytes compresses Chinese messages to one third.
These two channels do not truncate bodies, so the entire batch counts as delivered.
Verify indirectly through the renderer: unlimited markdownBody(0) retains everything.
TestMarkdownEscapesUntrustedContent is a regression test that untrusted content cannot alter message structure.
Titles and summaries come from model output informed by target responses; asset names come from target URLs.
Must appear in the result, escaped.
Must not appear in the result, unescaped.
Fold newlines to prevent forged list items or blockquotes;
escape square brackets and parentheses to prevent clickable external links.
Single-item writeItem is the rendering path shared by three markdown channels.
TestMarkdownEscapeBackslashFirst locks down escape order: handle backslashes first,
or newly added backslashes are escaped again, producing double backslashes.
TestTelegramTitleHasNoMarkdownEscapes locks down a specific regression:
markdown escaping must not leak into Telegram HTML (previously the shared title function
escaped titles, producing visible backslashes such as `\(1\)` in Telegram messages).
This file tests the invariant that **no** error text from channel implementations may contain credentials.
Why a separate file: initial channel tests covered only success and platform business errors,
not transport failures, which are the most dangerous (connection refusal / DNS failure / timeout).
http.Client.Do returns *url.Error including the **complete URL**, while provider
credentials are in that URL. The error exposed credentials through four outlets:
notification_deliveries.last_error -> plaintext storage.
GET /api/notify/deliveries responses -> bypass configuration masking and echo to the browser.
Server logs -> often forwarded for retention.
Test-send endpoint 502 responses -> displayed directly in the frontend.
Rather than testing only one function, each channel makes a real request guaranteed to fail; assert that error text
does not contain the credential.
credentialCases covers all channel shapes with credentials in URLs:
DingTalk/WeCom in query, Feishu in the final path segment, Telegram in the middle path segment.
leakProbeToken is a sentinel that cannot be a real credential, searched for in error text.
TestChannelErrorsNeverLeakCredentials is the core invariant.
Guaranteed-failure peer: nothing listens on 127.0.0.1:1, exercising connection refusal.
TestChannelErrorsNeverLeakCredentialsInPermanentPath covers permanent failures:
URL validation and platform business errors also expose text and must not contain credentials.
Credential-bearing but malformed URL -> exercise validateHTTPURL / url.Parse.
The redacted result must contain no original path/query fragments.
Never echo the original unparseable input.
TestRedactTransportErrorStripsURL directly checks *url.Error:
it is the return type from http.Client.Do and the original source of the leak.
Preserve Op too (POST versus GET helps diagnosis).
TestRedactURLsInTextHandlesFallback covers non-*url.Error custom errors:
URLs in redirect-policy errors and similar errors must also be removed.
Preserve text without URLs unchanged.
TestCrossHostRedirectRefused covers credentials in URLs plus cross-host redirects exposing those credentials.
Two httptest servers use different 127.0.0.1 ports; different ports mean different Host values,
which constitutes a cross-host redirect.
TestSameHostRedirectAllowed is the inverse: same-host redirects, such as adding a slash, must remain usable,
or normal workflows would also be blocked.
Redirect on the same host and port.
The package's most important invariant: WeCom limits **bytes**, Chinese takes 3 bytes per character,
and hard byte slicing can split characters, producing invalid UTF-8 rejected by the platform.
Use mixed Chinese/English inputs with coprime lengths to exercise every possible cut point.
Four-byte emoji make incorrect cuts more obvious.
Do not alter content when no truncation is needed.
When max is shorter than the ellipsis, adding the ellipsis must not exceed the limit.
Normally include an ellipsis.
Keep the distinction from TruncateBytes: Telegram limits characters,
whereas counting bytes would retain only one third of Chinese messages.
The same string measured in bytes should be substantially shorter.
The truncated result must remain readable and valid.
Direct HTML truncation can leave fragments such as `<a href="htt`, causing rejection of the entire message.
No unclosed trailing `<` (the final fragment cannot have `<` without `>`).
Beyond the asset limit, show the total count so readers know how many are omitted.
Echo unknown statuses unchanged; do not invent labels.
TestTruncateHTMLNeverCutsEntity covers an audit finding: truncation must avoid
partial HTML entities as well as partial tags.
Cutting `&` to `&amp` may cause an entity-only parser to reject the **whole** message;
oversized batch messages are common, making that too costly.
No partial trailing entity with & but no corresponding ;.
Signature reference values were independently computed with OpenSSL, not this package's implementation;
otherwise tests prove only unchanged code, not correct algorithms.
DingTalk: printf '%s\n%s' "$TS" "$SECRET" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$SECRET" -binary | openssl base64 -A
Feishu: printf '' | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$(printf '%s\n%s' "$TS" "$SECRET")" -binary | openssl base64 -A
Signing must not overwrite existing query parameters (access_token).
TestSignAlgorithmsDiffer locks down the providers' reversed parameter roles:
DingTalk key=secret, Feishu key=string-to-sign; copying the other's algorithm necessarily fails verification.
This test prevents a future refactor from merging them into one function.
Bots without signing must not acquire timestamp/sign parameters.
Do not permit file:// and similar schemes; http.Client behavior for them exceeds the intended scope.
This file covers two related hardening measures:
1. Delivery URLs must not use the server as a relay to internal networks / cloud metadata (SSRF).
2. URL validation errors must not expose credentials embedded in URLs.
Test environment: many tests use httptest receivers on 127.0.0.1, blocked by default.
TestMain enables AllowLocalTargetsEnv globally, and each SSRF test below explicitly
clears it to assert **default-deny** behavior.
Allow regular tests to reach fake local receivers; SSRF tests temporarily clear this themselves.
TestDialGuardRejectsLoopbackByDefault is the core SSRF assertion:
default configuration must reject loopback delivery at the **connection layer**.
Disable the escape hatch = default behavior.
Errors should explain how to opt in (a local SMTP relay is legitimate).
TestDialGuardAllowsLoopbackWhenOptedIn is the inverse: explicit opt-in must work,
or legitimate local postfix / internal relay deployments would become unusable.
Cloud metadata endpoint: the main reason for this function.
Unmap IPv4-mapped forms before checking, or they provide a bypass.
RFC1918 private networks are **deliberately permitted**: internal Mattermost / SMTP relays are common legitimate uses.
This assertion preserves that tradeoff; adding a private-network check later makes it fail,
requiring a conscious decision rather than silently breaking deployments.
TestValidateHTTPURLRejectsLiteralPrivateTargets covers early configuration feedback:
reject literal IPs at save time instead of waiting for the first failed delivery.
Public and private network addresses still pass (private addresses are left to dialing, which permits them).
TestValidateHTTPURLErrorNeverLeaksCredentials covers the branch missed in the previous audit pass.
Failed url.Parse returns *url.Error containing the complete original URL. The earlier pass only
redacted http.Client.Do errors, missing this branch. Its permanent-failure tests
(file://, gopher://, ftp://) all parsed successfully and exercised scheme validation instead,
so green tests provided false assurance about this branch.
Invalid percent escape.
Nonnumeric port.
Unbalanced bracket.
First verify that this input **actually** makes url.Parse fail; otherwise it could unknowingly
exercise another branch, recreating the earlier false assurance.
Ensure channel-level wrapping does not expose the URL either.
TestEmailDialGuardRejectsLoopbackByDefault covers the SMTP dial guard.
Email previously used bare net.Dialer, the sole SSRF gap: host values
169.254.169.254 or 127.0.0.1 could connect directly, and failed smtp.NewClient handshakes included
the peer's response line in errors echoed through last_error and delivery history, providing the same
semi-blind read primitive already closed in other channels. Refusal-versus-timeout timing also enabled port probing.
TestMain globally enables AllowLocalTargetsEnv because many tests use fake receivers on 127.0.0.1,
so this test must clear it; otherwise it passes whether or not the guard exists,
which is why the original gap went undetected.
Disable the escape hatch = default behavior.
No connection should be established: the Control hook rejects it before EHLO can be sent.
Errors must explain how to opt in (a local postfix relay is legitimate).
TestEmailDialGuardAllowsLoopbackWhenOptedIn is the paired inverse: explicit opt-in
must permit normal delivery. Internal SMTP / local relays are common, legitimate deployments and must not be blanket-blocked.
This file locks down the generic Webhook template's **capability boundary**.
This is the package's only place evaluating user-supplied strings as code, so specify what templates can
and cannot do, and enforce those properties with tests. Otherwise adding a context
method or a readFile FuncMap function could silently expand capabilities while the diff
looks like a harmless helper.
TestTemplateContextHasNoMethods is the most important assertion.
text/template invokes exported methods ({{.Foo}} accesses fields or calls methods). Thus any
reachable type with exported methods exposes those methods to template authors.
This context deliberately contains only plain data: exported fields and no methods.
Failure means a method was added to webhookTemplateData / webhookItem.
Before permitting it, consider whether templates could use it to read unintended data.
TestTemplateFuncsAreMinimal locks down the exposed function set.
Every FuncMap entry adds a capability. Currently only json / jsons serialize values
to JSON fragments: no file access, requests, or command execution.
TestTemplateCannotReachUnknownData covers out-of-bounds template access:
accessing nonexistent data must fail rather than echo anything; errors must not expose internal data.
Errors must not include actual context content such as vulnerability titles/summaries.
TestTemplateRenderFailsPermanently: malformed templates are configuration errors, not repairable by retry.
If retryable, each delivery with a bad template wastes three backoff rounds.
Even direct delivery bypassing validation must classify this as permanent, not repeatedly retry.
TestTemplateCanOnlyProduceJSON enforces valid JSON template output.
It also prevents generating plaintext to trigger other protocols.
Valid templates pass.
Reject non-JSON output rather than sending it unchanged.
testPaths creates an isolated update directory. Do not use ResolvePaths(), which points at the test
binary itself and would rename the go test executable.
fakeBin writes an executable shell script standing in for artex. smokeTest only launches it with -h and checks its exit code;
a script suffices and is much faster than compiling a real binary.
stage prepares bin as staged for swapping by writing artex.new and its checksum.
build.sh strips v while tags include v; accept both.
Compare numerically, not lexicographically.
Development builds must be noncomparable, or stable releases could overwrite uncommitted changes.
Key invariant: all update files share the executable's directory. CWD would break service-mode swapping
when the working directory is /.
Windows .new/.old must retain .exe or smoke testing and post-swap execution fail.
Modify the file after writing its checksum to simulate corruption or replacement.
Executable but exits nonzero.
Keep the marker: the next startup runs the new version and uses it to count attempts and roll back if needed.
Corrupt the checksum.
Backup left by the previous update.
The first maxAttempts startups only count attempts, giving the new version a chance to stabilize.
One more crash exceeds the limit and automatically restores the old version.
Keep the unstartable version for diagnosis rather than deleting it.
Rollback() uses ResolvePaths(); directly test the underlying swap semantics here.
sha256sum separates with two spaces; shasum -a 256 binary mode prefixes filenames with *.
Exactly two fields, but the first is not a digest.
Incorrect digest length.
Normalize digests to lowercase to avoid case-only mismatches.
Real release layout: artex-<版本>-<os>-<arch>/artex, plus distracting files (naming notation preserved).
Not HTTPS.
Domain not allowlisted.
Deceptive suffix.
Domain matching is case-insensitive.
build.sh package_binary uses artex-<版本>-<os>-<arch>.zip, with the version
stripped of its v prefix. A one-character mismatch breaks asset discovery for updates on every platform.
Without the marker, normal future restarts neither count attempts nor spuriously trigger rollback.
Keep the backup so users can still roll back manually.
Normal startup must neither panic nor modify any files.
Reclamation runs in background chunks.
Must converge, not get stuck within the budget.
Three historical traffic entries, including a legacy path<>'' row.
---- New version takes over.
1. Must open the same file, not silently create a new empty database.
2. All historical data remains visible.
3. Historical full-text indexing remains searchable.
4. Historical bodies remain readable.
5. Do not misclassify the old database as supporting incremental reclamation.
6. Deletion still works and reclamation converges on the old database.
7. The legacy path<>'' row is unaffected.
Old binary takes over.
